content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published comprehensive guidelines in July 2021 to provide recommendations and guidance on self-testing for the hepatitis C virus (HCV). These guidelines aim to address the global challenge of diagnosing and treating HCV, which remains a significant public health issue despite the availability of effective and affordable treatments. WHO estimates that in 2019, 58 million people worldwide were living with chronic HCV infection, but only 21% of them were diagnosed. Barriers such as lack of awareness, limited access to testing and treatment, stigma, and discrimination contribute to the low uptake of HCV testing services. To eliminate HCV as a public health problem by 2030, WHO has set ambitious targets to diagnose 90% of individuals with chronic HCV and treat 80% of those eligible for treatment. Achieving these goals requires innovative approaches to reach undiagnosed individuals and link them to care. One such approach is HCV self-testing (HCVST), which allows individuals to collect their own specimens (blood or oral fluid), perform a rapid diagnostic test (RDT), and interpret the results in a private setting. This method is particularly valuable for populations who may not access traditional testing services. HCVST is not a diagnostic tool but serves as an initial screening method. Reactive results from self-testing must be confirmed through further testing by trained healthcare providers using national diagnostic algorithms. WHO recommends confirmatory testing with either HCV RNA or HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) tests to establish viremia and assess the need for treatment. The guidelines emphasize the importance of linking HCVST to post-test services, including confirmatory testing, treatment, care, and referral services, in accordance with national standards. They also highlight the need to adapt HCVST delivery to local contexts and community preferences. Engaging communities, particularly key and vulnerable populations, in the development, implementation, and monitoring of HCVST programs is crucial for their success. HCVST offers a private and convenient option for individuals who may prefer self-care approaches, including those from key populations such as men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or closed settings, transgender people, and sex workers. It can also expand access to testing in high-burden settings and among vulnerable groups, such as migrants and mobile populations from endemic regions. Service delivery models should be tailored to local epidemiology and community needs, offering users choices in how they access and use HCVST. The guidelines build on the success of HIV self-testing (HIVST), which has been widely implemented and proven effective in increasing testing uptake, particularly among populations that may not otherwise test. Lessons learned from HIVST have informed the development of HCVST guidelines, which aim to support countries in scaling up testing services and achieving the 2030 elimination targets. The primary audience for these guidelines includes policymakers, program managers, healthcare providers, and community-based organizations, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The guidelines also serve as a resource for donors, development agencies, and international organizations involved in planning and implementing HCV testing programs. By promoting equity, respecting human rights, and integrating HCV testing into universal health coverage frameworks, these guidelines aim to improve access to care and reduce the burden of HCV globally.
